production-ready code is a challenge every developer knows well. Too often, the handoff from design to engineering leads to confusion, rework, or code that doesn’t quite match the intended UI. That’s where Figma’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) comes in. MCP acts as a bridge, giving AI-powered tools like Cursor direct access to your design’s underlying structure — not just its appearance — so they can generate code that truly reflects your design system and intent.</p><p id="d021" class="pw-post-body-paragraph me mf gl mg b mh mi mj mk ml mm mn mo mp mq mr ms mt mu mv mw mx my mz na nb ge cv" data-selectable-paragraph="">In this guide, I’ll show you exactly how to connect Figma with Cursor using MCP. I’ll cover everything from initial setup in both tools to solving common integration issues. Along the way, I’ll share practical examples with Github code that highlight how this workflow can save time, reduce errors, and finally make design-to-code handoff as seamless as it should be.</p><p id="d636" class="pw-post-body-paragraph me mf gl mg b mh mi mj mk ml mm mn mo mp mq mr ms mt mu mv mw mx my mz na nb ge cv" data-selectable-paragraph=""><strong class="mg gm">What is MCP?</strong></p><p id="7704" class="pw-post-body-paragraph me mf gl mg b mh mi mj mk ml mm mn mo mp mq mr ms mt mu mv mw mx my mz na nb ge cv" data-selectable-paragraph="">MCP, or Model Context Protocol, is an open standard designed to let large language models (LLMs) communicate directly with external tools, systems, and data sources. Instead of working in isolation, AI applications can use MCP to fetch real-time information, trigger workflows, or interact with platforms beyond their own environment — making them far more capable
